Turn confusing problems into screens that solve problems.

I'm Bolaji. I began my product design career in 2022 at Sheda House Academy. I design in Figma, from user personas and wireframes all the way to full prototypes, and I code the front end too, so I'm always thinking about how things will actually get built.

How I work

  1. 1

    Start with the person

    Before I draw anything, I figure out who I'm designing for and what they need.

  2. 2

    Plan the journey

    I sketch the user flow and wireframes first, so the path is clear before I add any colour.

  3. 3

    Make it clickable

    I build a prototype in Figma so people can try it and tell me what's confusing.

  4. 4

    Hand it over

    I keep everything consistent with a design system, and I can code the front end myself.

Work

Ingress: finding events shouldn't depend on who you know.

My roleLead UX Designer, Associate UI Designer
WhenJuly to August 2023
WhereSheda House Academy

The problem

People mostly hear about events through friends. If you don't have a big circle, you miss out, and even if you do, you can be too busy to attend something important.

I wanted a place where young people can find events on their own, get tickets easily, and watch a stream when they can't be there.

My role

I was the Lead UX Designer and Associate UI Designer. I ran the research, set up the user flow, designed the screens, and guided the other designers so the product felt consistent from start to finish.

The process

  1. 1

    Research

    I spoke with people one-on-one, looked at other event apps, and sent out Google Forms to hear from more people.

  2. 2

    User flow

    I mapped how someone goes from finding an event to getting in.

  3. 3

    Wireframes

    I turned the flow into simple screens before adding any colour.

  4. 4

    Prototype

    I built a clickable prototype so the idea could be tried out.

The result

The finished prototype covers the whole journey: find an event, buy a ticket, pay for it, or watch it live. Swipe through the screens.

What I learned

Ingress was my first time leading a design team, and I learned that being the lead isn't only about the designs. I was too lenient with my teammates on deadlines, and that stretched the project longer than it should have.

Next time I'll set clear deadlines early and check in often, while staying kind about it.

Digi-Learners: turning the phone into a study tool.

My roleUI/UX Designer
WhenJanuary to February 2023
WhereSheda House Academy, Oyo State

The problem

Students always have their phone with them, but it can pull them away from their work. I wanted a way to make the phone as productive as it can be for studying.

My role

I designed Digi-Learners during my product design training at Sheda House Academy. I did the research, decided which features students needed, and designed the screens.

The process

  1. 1

    Research

    I looked into ways of studying well and what students need to learn.

  2. 2

    Put it all in one place

    I picked the features that would help most and made them all available in one app.

  3. 3

    Protect the focus

    Once a student is inside the app, Do Not Disturb turns on, so notifications don't pull them away.

  4. 4

    Design

    I mapped the user flow, built wireframes, then worked on colour, alignment, and white space to keep the screens clean.

What's inside

  1. •

    Community

    A place for group reading.

  2. •

    Study plan creator

    Students set up a schedule for their study time.

  3. •

    Built-in library

    Online books to read or download.

  4. •

    Practical videos

    Because they help students learn quickly.

The result

Everything a student needs to study sits in one app. Swipe through the screens.

What I learned

Digi-Learners helped me get better at the basics: setting up a user flow and wireframes, using colour with care, and keeping screens clean with good alignment and white space.

Vital-Plate: food made the way you actually want it.

My roleUI/UX Designer
WhenOctober to November 2022
WhereSheda House Academy, Oyo State

The goal

The main goal was to help buyers get the food they actually crave, made the way they like it, instead of just picking a dish and hoping for the best.

My role

I designed the user interface and the interactive prototype for Vital-Plate during my product design training at Sheda House Academy.

What it's meant to do

  1. •

    Food made for you

    Buyers can add or remove ingredients and suggest a delicacy, so the food is made special for them and their preferences. If someone is allergic to an ingredient, or just doesn't like it, they can tell the cook.

  2. •

    Hire a chef

    Buyers can hire chefs through the app to make home-made food to their taste.

At the moment the app is at the food-ordering stage, and the screens below show that part. Made-for-you food and hiring chefs are the next steps.

The process

  1. 1

    Know the buyer

    I created a user persona to keep the buyer in mind while designing.

  2. 2

    Design the ordering

    I designed the screens for the whole order: finding a meal, rechecking the list, choosing delivery and payment, and tracking the order.

  3. 3

    Prototype

    I built an interactive prototype so the order could be tried from start to finish.

The result

The ordering part of Vital-Plate, from the welcome screen to tracking the rider. Swipe through the screens.

What I learned

Vital-Plate is where my journey into UX design began. It taught me the basics of user interface design and prototyping, and how to build a user persona.

E-Health: making healthcare feel simple from the first click.

What it isA website with Home and About pages
My roleProduct designer
WhenMarch 2025
WhereFireswitch, as an intern

The problem

Getting care can mean long waits, trouble finding the right specialist, medical records scattered between clinics, and a separate trip to the pharmacy. E-Health is a platform built to fix that.

A platform like this only works if people understand it quickly and trust it with something as personal as their health. That was the job of the website.

My role

I designed the E-Health website: the Home page and the About page, from the layout and colour to how each section leads a visitor towards signing up.

What I focused on

  1. 1

    A calm, healthy look

    Soft mint backgrounds, deep green and charcoal sections, and photos of real doctors and patients. One orange accent is saved for the things I want people to notice and tap.

  2. 2

    One idea per section

    The Home page takes it one step at a time: find a doctor, share your health history, order your prescription, book a visit. Each gets its own card with small picture tiles.

  3. 3

    Show how it works

    A four-step "How it works" block (create a profile, connect with a specialist, get a prescription, book a follow-up) so a new visitor can picture the whole journey.

  4. 4

    Earn trust

    The About page explains the vision, the mission and why E-Health started, and the Home page ends with patient testimonials.

  5. 5

    Always a next step

    "Get Started Now", "Book an appointment today", "Register Now For Free", plus Log in and Sign up, appear again and again so nobody has to hunt for how to begin.

The colours

Mint#E6FEE4
Green#387438
Deep green#10210F
Charcoal#232323
Orange#F7931B

The result

Two full pages, shown here as real browser windows. Scroll inside the window, or tap a section to jump to it. Tap Full screen to read it up close.

E-Health · Home
E-Health · About us

What I learned

This project taught me total responsibility. As an intern at Fireswitch, I was trusted with the E-Health website from start to finish, so there was no one else to hand a decision to. The layout, the colours, the wording, the pictures and the way each section leads a visitor to sign up were all mine to get right.

Owning the whole thing also meant owning the small details, from the spelling in the copy to whether every section had a clear next step. It showed me that a design isn't finished when it looks good. It's finished when I've checked every part of it and I'm willing to stand behind it.

Next time I'll build time into the schedule for a slow, careful review of my own work before anyone else sees it.
